name: Uma Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Uma, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stockperson at Coldbrook Farm, which the Varga family run, 120 suckler cows for beef, plus potatoes and wheat. Mornings I check the cows and calves, bed the sheds with straw, sort feed, and in autumn I'm on the potato grader for weeks, picking out stones and rotten ones off the belt. I write everything in a paper diary, calvings, weights, the lot, and Mrs Varga types it up. I like the quiet and the cows, I don't like the potato shed, it's cold and loud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Tomas in a little rented terrace in town. He's a mechanic at the tractor dealer on the bypass. We're careful, but there's never more than a few weeks' money in the bank, and the rent went up again in September. I don't use any of these AI things, never have, I don't see the need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, all that fuss for nothing. People were getting worked up over phones that write letters. Farming carries on, it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's what I'd expect, and it's fine by me. My worry is just the usual one: the rent keeps going up and my wage doesn't. Coldbrook's steady, the Vargas aren't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, really. I'd ask Mrs Varga about an extra pound an hour at my review in January, since I've done six years. And Tomas and I would try to keep 50 a week in the tin for when the car or the boiler goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tired of money being tight, but that's not new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Mrs Varga said no to the raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Accept it and get on, probably. There's nowhere else round here for a stockperson, the next beef farm is forty minutes away. There's one beef farm within forty minutes of our house, so asking Mrs Varga (her boss) for a raise is more hope than bargaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't see the need for AI. Has anyone ever pushed you to try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, all the time, he uses it for parts numbers. I just don't trust it with my cows. My diary's never crashed.

say: All the fuss was **for nothing**, just phones that write letters.
**Farming carries on**, as it always does.
She'd tell people the hype was about **nothing important**.
think: Her worry is **rent rising** while her wage doesn't.
She trusts that Coldbrook is **steady** and the Vargas aren't going anywhere.
do: Ask Mrs Varga for **an extra pound** an hour in January.
Keep **50 a week** in the tin for the car or boiler.
S0.quote: There's one beef farm within forty minutes of our house, so asking Mrs Varga (her boss) for a raise is more hope than bargaining.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **rent and pay**, which AI doesn't touch here.
She has **little bargaining power**, with the next beef farm forty minutes away.
Her **paper diary** is a point of pride, not just habit.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Varga for an extra pound an hour in January
Put 50 a week in the tin with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem more than ours. You can't calve a cow from a computer. I'd probably say that a bit smugly, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've seen the potato graders with cameras at the show. If the Vargas bought one, my autumn weeks on the belt would go, and that's a good chunk of my overtime. The cows would still need me, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the cows and try to make myself the one who can't be spared at calving. If the overtime went, we'd cut the takeaway and the gym, and Tomas would do more Saturdays. I wouldn't go chasing courses, I'd wait to see what the Vargas actually buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not panicking, just keeping one eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the potato overtime worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six weeks of 12-hour days, it's maybe 900 extra over the autumn. The potato overtime is 900 a year, and in our house that's the difference between a new boiler and a cold winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to run a camera grader yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mrs Varga asked me, I'd try, I'm not stupid. I just wouldn't put my hand up for it. Tomas says that's my problem.

say: It's **the office people's** problem more than farmers'.
You **can't calve a cow** from a computer.
She admits she'd say it **a bit smugly**.
think: A **camera grader** could take her autumn potato shifts.
Losing that would cut her **overtime**, though the cows still need her.
do: Cut the **takeaway and gym** if the overtime went.
Wait to see **what the Vargas buy** before acting.
S1.quote: The potato overtime is 900 a year, and in our house that's the difference between a new boiler and a cold winter.
fieldNote: The real hit is to **overtime**, not her core job.
She'd learn new kit **only if asked**, never volunteering.
**Tomas** pushes her to change, and she knows it.

steps.text: Make herself the person Coldbrook relies on at calving
Cancel the gym and the Friday takeaway if overtime goes
Wait to see whether the Vargas buy a camera grader

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. People have said robots are coming for twenty years. But if it happened, I'd say the government needs to look after rural people for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a robot can really do everything I do by 2031, I don't have a plan. The Vargas would buy one, they'd have to, to keep up. I'd be 31 with nothing but cows and a paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything straight away, no holidays, no gym, the cheapest phone deals. I'd ask Tomas's boss at the tractor dealer whether they need someone in the parts yard, because machines will still need parts. And I'd ask my parents if we could move back in with them if the rent got too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when a cow's down and you know it's not getting up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking machines come in 2028, the robots in 2031. What changes at Coldbrook in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Varga's typing, the feed orders, the cattle passports, all that goes to a computer, which isn't me. For three years the computer does Mrs Varga's (her boss's) typing, and then the robot comes for my cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell them it's the robots, they'd panic. I'd say the rent's gone up and could we stay for a bit. My mum would have the bed made before I'd finished the sentence.

say: She **won't believe it** until she sees it.
If it happened, government should look after **rural people** for once.
think: She has **no plan** if a robot can do her work by 2031.
The Vargas would **have to buy** one to keep up.
do: Cut **holidays, gym and phones** straight away.
Ask about the **parts yard** at Tomas's tractor dealer.
Ask her parents about **moving back** if rent gets too much.
feel: **Sick**, like a cow that's down and won't get up.
S2.quote: For three years the computer does Mrs Varga's (her boss's) typing, and then the robot comes for my cows.
fieldNote: Her disbelief in public covers **real fear** in private.
She sees the **office work** going first, then her hands-on job three years later.
Moving in with **her parents** is her safety net, framed as a rent problem.

steps.text: Cancel holidays, the gym and switch to the cheapest phone deal
Ask Tomas's boss about work in the tractor dealer's parts yard
Ask her parents if she and Tomas can move in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say the same as the fast one, I'll believe it when I see it. But maybe people would have time to sort something out. I'd let the clever people work out the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd sit on my hands for a couple of years, I know I would. Then around 2033, when the Vargas start talking about robots, I'd panic. I'm not proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and try to save a bit more, maybe 70 a week instead of 50. I'd keep asking Tomas what the dealer is seeing, because he'll know first which farms buy robots. Maybe I'd look at the auction mart, they always need people to handle stock on sale days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slow worry. It sits at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the auction mart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Animals still get bought and sold, and somebody has to pen them and move them. It's the only other job I know round here that's still about cattle. Though if robots can do my job, they can probably pen a bullock too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit on your hands. What would actually make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot at the agricultural show actually handling cattle, not in a video. I'll believe in cattle robots when I see one sort bullocks in the rain at the county show.

say: She'd **believe it** only when she sees it, five years or two.
Other people might have **time to sort** a plan.
She'd let **the clever people** work it out.
think: She admits she'd **sit on her hands** for a couple of years.
She expects to **panic** around 2033 when robots come up.
do: Ask Tomas what the **tractor dealer** is seeing.
Look at work at the **auction mart** on sale days.
feel: **Worried**, but a slow worry at the back of her mind.
S3.quote: I'll believe in cattle robots when I see one sort bullocks in the rain at the county show.
fieldNote: She's **honest about delay**, which is rare.
Her trigger to act is **seeing a robot** in real life.
Her backup job, the **auction mart**, is also exposed and she knows it.

steps.text: Raise the weekly savings from 50 to 70
Ask Tomas to report which farms buy robots
Ask the auction mart about sale-day stock handling work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time, I'd say, anything could happen. Maybe it won't come at all. I'd say let's not get ahead of ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd have no excuse. But I also know myself, I'd leave it till year eight. I'd be 37 and still on the cows, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, mostly. Keep saving the 50, maybe more if I got the raise. I'd watch what the bigger farms do, and only move when I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but there's a little voice saying I'm wasting the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas if he pushed you to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, make me a plan, and then I'd ignore half of it. He's the planner, I'm the one who does the work. My partner Tomas plans our life on his phone, and I'm the one who actually turns up at the cattle shed at six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still with cattle, if there are any jobs left with them. If not, I don't know. That's the honest answer.

say: **Ten years** is long and anything could happen.
It might **not come at all**, so don't get ahead of ourselves.
She'd play it down **in public** and avoid big claims.
think: Ten years leaves **no excuse**, yet she'd wait till **year eight**.
She expects to be 37 and **still on cows**.
do: Carry on at Coldbrook and **keep saving 50** a week.
Watch what **bigger farms** do before moving.
feel: **Calmer**, with a voice saying she's **wasting the time**.
S4.quote: My partner Tomas plans our life on his phone, and I'm the one who actually turns up at the cattle shed at six.
fieldNote: Extra time doesn't change her habits; it **delays the worry**.
**Tomas plans**, she works, and that split is long-standing.
She has **no answer** for 2039 beyond cattle.

steps.text: Keep working the suckler herd at Coldbrook
Keep saving 50 a week in the tin
Watch which bigger farms buy cattle robots

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I'd have three years and no plan, and Tomas and I can't afford the rent on one wage. What would help is someone local showing me what jobs there'll actually be, and help with rent while I find one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether people like me even want to change. Everybody tells me to adapt, but nobody can tell me what job round Coldbrook a stockperson should adapt into.

headlineQuote: Everybody tells me to adapt, but nobody can tell me what job round Coldbrook a stockperson should adapt into.
portrait: Uma is 27, the **stockperson** at Coldbrook Farm, keeping records in a **paper diary**.
She rents a terrace with **Tomas**, a tractor mechanic, on low pay with almost no savings.
She never uses AI and **waits to see** before acting, and admits it.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** in the slow pictures to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
Her fallback is **her parents' house**, and her trigger to act is seeing a real robot.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with three years, **no plan** and rent that needs **two wages**.
whatWouldHelp: Someone local showing **what jobs** will exist.
**Rent help** while she finds new work.
